documents.text:
S.I. 49 of 2023
217
Statutory Instrument 49 of 2023.
[CAP. 20:27
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023
ARRANGEMENT OF SECTIONS
Section

	 1.	 Title.
	 2.	 Interpretation.
	 3.	 Application.
	 4.	 Prohibited substances and equipment.
	 5.	 Import, export and transit licences.
	 6.	 Processing of application and issuance of licences.
	 7.	 Suspension or cancellation of licences.
	 8.	 Amendment and replacement of licences.
	 9.	 Register of licensed importers, exporters and transit good licensees.
10.	Returns to be furnished by licensed importers, exporters or
consumers.
11.	 Authorised persons to service, repair, handle, install and
decommission ozone depleting substances, greenhouse gases,
greenhouse gases dependent equipment and ozone depleting
substances dependent equipment.
12.	Permission to destroy ozone depleting substances, greenhouse
gases, greenhouse gases dependent equipment and ozone depleting
substances dependent equipment.
13.	Labelling, packaging, “proof of origin” and energy performance.
14.	Repeal.

First Schedule: Forms.

Second Schedule: List of Prohibited Ozone Depleting Substances.

Third Schedule: List of Controlled Substances: Ozone Depleting
Substances.

Fourth Schedule: List of Controlled Substances: Greenhouse
Gases.
DISTRIBUTED BY VERITAS
e-mail: veritas@mango.zw; website: www.veritaszim.net
Veritas makes every effort to ensure the provision of reliable information,
but cannot take legal responsibility for information supplied.
218
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023

Fifth Schedule: List of Controlled ODS and GHG Dependent
Equipment.

Sixth Schedule: Fees.

IT is hereby notified that the Minister of Environment, Climate,
Tourism and Hospitality Industry has, in terms of section 140(2)(b)
of the Environmental Management Act [Chapter 20:27] made the
following regulations:—
Title

1. These regulations may be cited as the Environmental
Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone Depleting Substances,
Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting Substance Dependent Equipment
and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment) Regulations, 2023.
Interpretation

2. In these regulations—

“enforcement officer” means an officer appointed in terms
of section 35(1) of the Environmental Management Act
[Chapter 20:27] or any other  officer appointed by the
Secretary for the Ministry responsible for ozone layer
protection to enforce the provisions of these  regulations;

“form” means the appropriate form as specified in the First
Schedule;

“greenhouse gas” or “GHG”, means any Hydrofluorocarbons
or mixtures of Hydrofluorocarbons controlled by and
listed under the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal
Protocol and specified in the Fourth Schedule;

“greenhouse gas dependent equipment” or “GHG dependent
equipment” means products or equipment consisting of
Hydrofluocarbons or mixtures of Hydrofluorocarbons,
including equipment whose continuous functioning
relies on the use of these gases;

“hydrocarbon” or “HC” means any organic chemical
containing Hydrogen and Carbon atoms with a zero
ozone depletion potential and low global warming
S.I. 49 of 2023
219
potential adopted as a replacement for ozone depleting
substances and greenhouse gases;

“Kigali Amendment” refers to an amendment of the Montreal
protocol that was effected at the 28th Meeting of Parties
and listed hydroflourocarbons as controlled substances;

“licence” means an import or export or transit licence issued
in terms of section 6 of these regulations;

“Montreal Protocol” means the Montreal Protocol on
Substances that Deplete the Ozone layer;

“officer” means a Zimbabwe Revenue Authority officer
appointed in terms of section 20 of the Revenue Authority
Act [Chapter 23:11];

“ozone depleting substance” or “ODS”, means any chemical
substance which destroys the ozone layer and is
controlled under the Montreal Protocol;

“ozone depleting substance dependent equipment” or “ODS
dependent equipment” means products or equipment
consisting of ozone depleting substances, including
equipment whose continuous functioning relies on the
use of ozone depleting substances;

“ozone office” means the National Ozone Office as established
by the Minister;

“quota” means maximum allowable quantities of an ozone
depleting substance or a greenhouse gas which an
applicant is allowed to import or export within a calendar
year;

“secretary” means Permanent Secretary for the Ministry
responsible for the protection of the ozone layer.
Application

3.  These regulations shall apply to private and public individuals,
industrial and commercial importers, exporters, producers and
consumers of ozone depleting substances and greenhouse gases
listed in the Second, Third and Fourth Schedules and ozone depleting
substance and greenhouse gas dependent equipment listed in the Fifth
Schedule.
220
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023
Prohibited substances and equipment

4. (1) No person shall import into Zimbabwe, any substances
listed, and equipment or appliance which uses or whose continuous
function relies on the substances listed in the Second Schedule.

(2) No person shall import into Zimbabwe, any equipment
or appliance which uses or whose continuous function relies on
Dichlorofluoromethane (HCFC-22).

(3) Any person who contravenes subsections (1) and (2) shall
be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding level 14 or
imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year or both such fine
and such imprisonment.

(4) In addition, the court convicting a person of an offence
under subsection (1), may, upon the application of the Prosecutor,
declare any ozone depleting substances, greenhouse gases, greenhouse
gas dependent equipment or ozone depleting substance dependent
equipment in respect of which the offence has been committed to be
forfeited to the State.

(5)  Any ozone depleting substance, greenhouse gas and
ozone depleting substance or greenhouse gas dependent equipment
forfeited in terms of subsection (4) shall be destroyed or otherwise
dealt with as the Secretary may direct.

(6) The licence of any person or entity convicted in
contravention of subsection (1) may be terminated by the Secretary
or any person so delegated.
Import, export and transit goods licences

5. (1) Not less than one month prior to the commencement of
a new calendar year, the Ozone Office shall, through a notice in the
Gazette and at least two (2) newspapers enjoying wide circulation,
invite applications from individuals and companies intending to
import, transit or export ozone depleting substances, greenhouse gases,
ozone depleting substance dependent appliances and greenhouse gas
dependent appliances to submit applications in the prescribed form
to the office stating their projected requirements for the coming year.
S.I. 49 of 2023
221

(2)  Any person who wishes to import or export ozone depleting
substance, greenhouse gas, ozone depleting substance dependent
equipment or greenhouse gas dependent equipment or any chemical
listed in the Third and Fourth Schedules shall respond to the Ozone
Office’s advertisement and apply through the established online system
on the Government E-Services portal.

(3) Any person who wishes to transport ozone depleting
substances, greenhouse gases, ozone depleting substances dependent
equipment or greenhouse gas dependent equipment or any substances
listed in the Third, Fourth and Fifth Schedules in transit to neighbouring
countries shall apply through the established online system on the
Government E-Services portal.

(4) Any application for a licence made in terms of subsections
(2) and (3), shall be accompanied by an application fee as specified
in the Sixth Schedule, which is non-refundable.

(5) Where an applicant makes an application outside of the
timeline outlined in subsection (1) such application shall be considered
as a late application and will attract an additional non-refundable fee
constituting fifty (50) per centum of the application fee and can only
be processed subject to availability of allowable quotas in line with
the country’s ozone depleting substances phase out schedules and
greenhouse gases phase down schedules.
Processing of applications and issuance of licences

6. (1) The Ozone Office shall, as soon as practicable, but in any
case not later than fourteen (14) working days from the date of receipt
of an application—

(a)	 grant the application and allocate an annual quota
(subject to such conditions as it may think fit to impose)
and issue to the applicant the import or export license
applied for; or

(b)	 refuse the application giving reasons thereof.

(2) If an application for a licence is successful (whether
approved with or without conditions by the Ozone Office), the Ozone
Office shall—

(a)	 inform the applicant accordingly; and
222
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023

(b)	 issue to the applicant a licence; and

(c)	 make an appropriate entry in the licensing register.

(3) Every licence shall be valid for a period of a calendar
year ending on 31st December of the year in which the applicant
received the licence, unless it is earlier surrendered to or cancelled
by the Ozone Office.

(4) If a licensee ceases to operate as such, he or she shall,
within thirty (30) days of ceasing to operate, surrender his or her
licence to the Ozone Office.

(5) Any person who contravenes subsection (4) shall be guilty
of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding level 5 or imprisonment
for a period not exceeding one month or both such fine and such
imprisonment.

(6) Where the Ozone Office issues a licence in terms of
subsection (1), the license shall state the allocated quota for each
controlled substance.

(7) No licence issued in terms of these regulations shall be
transferable to another person.

(8) Any person who contravenes subsection (7) shall be
guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding level 10 or
imprisonment for a period not exceeding one year or both such fine
and such imprisonment.

(9) All imported ozone depleting substances, greenhouse
gases and ozone depleting substance or greenhouse gas dependent
equipment shall be utilised before their phase out dates.

(10) All transit ozone depleting substances, greenhouse gases
and ozone depleting substance or greenhouse gas dependent equipment
shall be declared and certified at the exit port.
Suspension or cancellation of licences

7. (1) Subject to subsections (2) and (4),  the Ozone Office may
at any time suspend (for a period not exceeding sixty (60) days) or
cancel any licence if the Ozone Office has reasonable grounds for
believing that—
S.I. 49 of 2023
223

(a)	 the licence was issued in error or through fraud or
misrepresentation or non-disclosure of a material fact
by the licensee; or

(b)	 the licensee has contravened any provision of the Act or
these regulations or any condition of his or her licence;
or

(c)	 the licensee has ceased the licensed importation or
exportation.

(2) The Ozone Office shall notify the licensee in writing of
its intention to suspend or cancel his or her licence and the reasons
for doing so, and shall call upon the licensee to show cause, within
fourteen (14) days from the date of the notice, why the licence should
not be suspended or cancelled, as the case may be:

Provided that if in the opinion of the Ozone Office the licence
needs to be immediately suspended or cancelled in the public interest
or to avert an environmental emergency he or she can issue the notice
requiring the licensee to show cause after suspending or cancelling
the licence.

(3) If, at the expiry of the period specified in the notice given
in terms of subsection (2), and after considering any representations
made by the licensee, the Ozone Office is satisfied for any reason
specified in subsection (1) that the licence concerned should be
suspended or cancelled, the Ozone Office shall, by notice in writing
to the licensee, suspend or cancel the licence or take such other action
as it considers appropriate.

(4) The penalty of suspension is only available where there has
been a contravention of any provision of the Act or these regulations
or any condition of a licence which, in the opinion of the Ozone
Office, is a contravention that can be easily or speedily remediated
by the licensee:

Provided that—

(a)	 if after the expiry of the period of suspension the licensee
has not taken the remedial action, the Ozone Office shall
forthwith cancel the licence; or

(b) on good cause shown by the licensee, the Ozone Office
may extend the suspension for a period not exceeding
224
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023
thirty (30) days to allow the licensee to take the required
remedial action.

(5)  The Ozone Office shall immediately make an appropriate
entry in the register of licences where he or she suspends or lifts a
suspension of any licence or cancels it in accordance with this section.
Amendment and replacement of licences

8. (1) The Ozone Office may at any time amend a licence or
any terms or conditions of a licence—

(a)	 to correct any error in the licence; or

(b)	 if the licensee requests the amendment; or

(c) if it considers the amendment necessary to reflect the
true nature of the licensed activities; or

(d)	 if for any other reason it considers the amendment
necessary or desirable in the interests of the environment
or in the public interest.

(2) The Ozone Office shall notify the licensee in writing of
its intention to amend a licence on a ground referred to in subsections
(1)(a), (c) or (d) and shall call upon the licensee to show cause, within
14 days from the date of the notice, why the licence should not be
amended.

(3) Where a licensee requests an amendment to his or her
licence, he or she shall make an application to the Ozone Office in
Form AP2, together with the fee as specified in the Sixth Schedule.

(4) If in the opinion of the Ozone Office the amendment
sought by the licensee is a material amendment, section 6(2), (3),
(4), (5) and (6) shall apply as if the application for the amendment is
an original application for a licence.

(5)  Where a licence is lost or destroyed, the licensee may
apply to the Ozone Office in Form AP3, together with the fee as
specified in the Sixth Schedule, for a replacement licence:

Provided that, if the licensee finds the lost licence he or she
shall forthwith surrender it to the Ozone Office.
S.I. 49 of 2023
225

(6) Any person who contravenes the proviso to subsection (5)
shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not exceeding level 6
or imprisonment for a period not exceeding six months or both such
fine and such imprisonment.
Register of licensed importers, exporters and transit goods licensees

9. (1) The Ozone Office shall establish and maintain a register
of licences to be known as the Import, Export and Transit Goods
Licensing Register, which shall be for the purposes of registering
all licensed importers, exporters or consumers of ozone depleting
substances, greenhouse gases, ozone depleting substance dependent
equipment and greenhouse gas dependent equipment and in which
the following shall be recorded—

(a)	 the name and address of every licensee and the addresses
at which he or she operates from; and

(b)	 the allocated import or export quotas of each controlled
substance; and

(c)	 the date of issue of every licence and of any renewal
thereof; and

(d)	 any special  terms or conditions subject to which any
licence is issued or renewed; and

(e)	 the particulars of any suspension or cancellation or
amendment of the licence.

(2) Every licenced importer, exporter and transit goods
licensee shall pay registration fee specified in the Sixth Schedule to
be registered in the Import, Export and Transit Licensing Register
referred to in subsection (1).

(3) Any person may—

(a)	 inspect the register of licences free of charge at all
reasonable times at the premises of the Ozone Office
or at such other place that the Ozone Office may direct;
or

(b)	 obtain copies of or extracts from the register for a fee
as specified in the Sixth Schedule.

(4) The Ozone Office shall keep and maintain the register in
both material and electronic form.
226
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023
Returns to be furnished by licensed importers, exporters or consumers

10. (1) Every licensed importer or exporter of ozone depleting
substances, greenhouse gas, ozone depleting substances dependent
equipment or greenhouse gas dependent equipment shall in the
form and manner and within the time required by the Ozone Office,
furnish the Ozone Office with annual reports or other information in
connection with—

(a)	 quantities of ozone depleting substances, greenhouse
gases, ozone depleting substances dependent equipment
and greenhouse gas dependent equipment, imported or
exported, used or destroyed by approved means; and

(b)	 sources of each ozone depleting substance, greenhouse
gas, ozone depleting substance dependent equipment
and greenhouse gas dependent equipment, imported or
exported indicating country, address, contact person,
address and contact telephone or fax numbers; and

(c)	 quarterly or half-yearly inventories of ozone depleting
substance, greenhouse gas, ozone depleting substance
dependent equipment, greenhouse gas dependent
equipment indicating total capacity, consumed quantities
and projected imports or exports and consumption for
the following year.

(2) Any person who does not comply with the requirements
of subsection (1) shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not
exceeding level 6 or imprisonment for a period not exceeding six
months or both such fine and such imprisonment.
Authorised persons to repair, service, handle, install and
decommission ozone depleting substances, greenhouse gases,
ozone depleting substances dependent equipment and greenhouse
gas dependent equipment

11. (1) No person shall repair, service, handle, install or
decommission an ozone depleting substance, greenhouse gas, ozone
depleting substance dependent equipment and greenhouse gas
dependent equipment unless he or she has been trained and certified
S.I. 49 of 2023
227
to do any such activity by the National Ozone Office, in accordance
with the National Standard (SAZS 1012:2019) on certification of
refrigeration and air conditioning practitioners.

(2) Retailers, sellers and distributors of ozone depleting
substances and greenhouse gases, shall not sell such substances to any
person unless he or she has been trained and certified in the handling
of such substances by the National Ozone Office.

(3) The owner of the ozone depleting substance dependent
equipment or greenhouse gas dependent equipment with a rated charge
of ten (10) kilograms to be repaired, serviced, handled, installed or
decommissioned shall submit a written request to the National Ozone
Office before any work commences.

(4) The National Ozone Office shall supervise, monitor and
certify the recovery of refrigerant, installation or decommissioning
of ozone depleting substances dependent equipment or greenhouse
gas dependent equipment.

(5) Any person who contravenes the provisions of subsections
(1), (2) and (3) shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not
exceeding level 6 or imprisonment for a period not exceeding six
month or both such fine and such imprisonment.
Permission to destroy ozone depleting substances, greenhouse
gases, ozone depleting substance dependent equipment and
greenhouse gas dependent equipment

12. (1) If the owner or other person having control of ozone
depleting substances, greenhouse gases, ozone depleting substance
dependent equipment or greenhouse gas dependent equipment wishes
to destroy them, he or she shall submit a written statement to the
National Ozone Office.

(2) If the Ozone Office grants permission for the goods to be
destroyed, an enforcement officer shall be appointed to witness the
destruction and when the substance and equipment has been destroyed
the enforcement officer shall record the quantities destroyed and sign
a certificate of destruction.

(3) Any person who does not comply with the requirements
of subsection (1) shall be guilty of an offence and liable to a fine not
228
Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control of Ozone
Depleting Substances, Greenhouse Gases, Ozone Depleting
Substances and Greenhouse Gases Dependent Equipment)
Regulations, 2023
exceeding level 11 or imprisonment for a period not exceeding one
year or both such fine and such imprisonment.
Labelling, packaging, “proof of origin” and energy performance

13. (1) All importers, exporters  or consumers of ozone depleting
substances, greenhouse gases, ozone depleting substance dependent
equipment and greenhouse gas dependent equipment shall ensure
that such products are clearly labeled and packaged to national and
international standards.

(2)  The labels must state clearly, among other things, chemical
formulae, chemical name, safety measures, energy performance
levels, names and addresses of manufacturers, instructions for use
and disposal, United Nations number, Chemical Abstract Service
numbers and any other relevant information such as “ozone friendly”,
“climate friendly”, “ global warming”, or “ozone depleting”.

(3) All imported ozone depleting substances and greenhouse
gases to be used in refrigeration and air conditioning applications shall
be accompanied at the point of entry by a proof of origin signed by
a senior member of the producing company specifying the level of
purity of the substances, name and contact details of the company of
origin.

(4) Pursuant to subsections (1), (2), and (3) it shall be the
duty of an officer at all ports of entry, subject to any direction given
to him or her by the Secretary responsible for ozone layer protection
to ensure that all consignments are marked clearly, recording—

(a)	 the name, identity and quantity of imported or exported
ozone depleting substances or greenhouse gases; and

(b)	 details concerning contact address, labels and the
packaging; and

(c)	 any other particulars that may be required by the Ozone
Office.

(5) The officer shall not allow the importation of a substance
which has been phased out or an appliance containing a phased out
substance and any appliance that fails to meet the energy performance
S.I. 49 of 2023
229
levels stated in the National Standard (SAZ/IEC:62552) on minimum
energy performance of refrigeration and air conditioning appliances.

(6) Any person who does not comply with the requirements
of subsections (1), (2) and (3) shall be guilty of an offence and liable
to a fine not exceeding level 11 or imprisonment for a period not
exceeding six months or both such fine and such imprisonment
Repeal

14. The Environmental Management (Prohibition and Control
of Ozone Depleting Substances and Ozone Depleting Substance
Dependant Equipment) Regulations, 2016, published in Statutory
Instrument 131 of 2016, is hereby repealed.

Environmental Management Amendment
B
Environmental Management Amendment
i
ENVIRONMENTAL MANAGEMENT AMENDMENT BILL, 2026
_________________
Memorandum

This Bill will make amendments to the Environmental Management Act [Chapter
20:27]. In more detail, the individual clauses of the Bill provide as follows:—
Clause 1

This clause sets out the Bill’s short title.
Clause 2

This clause introduces new definitions and amendments to existing definitions
in the principal Act, of note is the definition of “environmental and social impact
assessment.” This has been proposed to ensure that assessments include a social
dimension to cover a broader spectrum of issues in line with environmental rights as
enshrined in the Constitution.
Clause 3

This clause makes an addition to the list of emerging international principles
on environmental law enshrined under section 4 of the principal Act. The principle
relates to the need for environmentally conscious production methods and encourages
management of waste at source or innovative measures which significantly reduce
waste produced to the benefit of the environment.
Clause 4

This clause seeks to operationalise the guiding principles of environmental law
enforcement laid out in the principal Act.
Clause 5

This clause sets out for the repeal of the provisions relating to the Environmental
Council as it has not served any purpose since inception. It has been found more prudent
to assign the Agency the functions that had been given to the Council.
Clauses 6, 7, 8 and 9

These clauses are aimed at aligning the composition of the Board with the Public
Entities Corporate Governance Act [Chapter 10:33], in terms of relevant qualifications
and managing the number of members, then also taking into consideration constitutional
provisions relating to gender balance.
Clause 10

This clause is aimed at aligning the Board provisions with constitutional provisions
related to gender balance with regard to the chairperson and vice chairperson of the
Board.
Clause 11

This clause provides for the repeal of the co-option of members into the Board.
Clause 12

This clause is aimed at aligning the principal Act with the Public Entities Corporate
Governance Act [Chapter 10:33] in relation to the appointment and term of office of
the Director-General.
Clause 13

This clause introduces a new provision into the principal Act to establish a
mandatory registration system for environmental service professionals. The objective
is to professionalise the environmental sector by ensuring that only qualified and
registered individuals provide services required under the Act.
(i)
Environmental Management Amendment
ii
Clause 14

This clause makes provision for tightened sanctions on offenders for failure to
adhere to an order issued by an environmental officer.
Clause 15

This clause provides for the issuance of civil penalty orders by the Agency.
Clause 16

This clause repeals sections 55 and 56. It has been realised that there is no need for
a Standards and Enforcement Committee. As such, the functions previously assigned
to this Committee are now being transferred to the Agency.
Clauses 17 and 18

These clauses provide for the Agency to penalise persons or authorities that discharge
effluents directly into the environment, especially in cases where local authority sewer
systems are not easily accessible or non-existent.
Clause 19

This clause provides for the repeal of the mention of the Standards and Enforcement
Committee wherever it appears and is substituted with the Agency.
Clause 20

This clause creates an offence where there is discharge of emissions without a
license from the Agency.
Clause 21

This clause gives the Agency power to charge a civil penalty on contravention of
the provision on discharge of waste.
Clause 22

This clause introduces a criminal sanction where there is discharge of hazardous
chemicals and materials, or oils, into the environment. This is required as the section
in the principal Act only contains a prohibition that does not have a sanction to it.
Clauses 23 and 24

These clauses introduce a criminal sanction to persons who are in the business of
manufacturing, importing, exporting, transporting, storing, selling, or use of hazardous
substances without a licence.
Clause 25

This clause introduces a criminal sanction to persons or authorities who do not
comply with the requirements set out for the collection of litter, as it provides for a
prohibition against littering and gives guidance as to what conditions must be met in
order to prevent littering.
Clause 26

This clause inserts a new provision related to the designation of priority waste. This
provision empowers the Minister to declare what is referred to as priority waste, where
the type of waste concerned poses a significantly increased threat to the environment.
Clause 27

This clause creates an offence where any specified authority fails to submit an
environmental management plan to the Agency or does not implement an approved
environmental management plan.
(ii)
Environmental Management Amendment
iii
Clauses 28 and 29

This makes provision for the requirement for organisations to notify the Agency
as well as carry out an environmental and social impact assessment where a previously
approved project is expanded.
Clause 30

This clause makes addition to the list of requirements that shall be contained in an
environmental and social impact assessment report, inclusive of a report of meaningful
consultations of affected and interested parties.
Clauses 31, 32, 33 and 34

These clauses make provision for certain conditions that attach to the approval
of an environmental and social impact assessment.
Clause 35

This clause provides for a new definition in Part XII, the definition of “environmental
purposes”.
Clause 36

This clause provides for the provisions in relation to appeals, by stating that an
appeal will not suspend a decision made by an inspector.
Clause 37

This clause provides for additional penalties for persons who hinders or obstructs
inspectors in carrying out their duties.
Clause 38

This clause makes liability of corporations and associations and their members,
employees and agencies. It also provides for non-prosecution agreements.
Clause 39

This clause adds on the functions of the Minister to make regulations by making
model by-laws and publish such model by-laws for the benefit and adoption of local
authorities.
Clause 40

This clause provides for the transitional provisions of any regulations, statutory
instruments, or notices made under the Environmental Management Act [Chapter
20:27] before the coming into operation of this Amendment.
Clause 41

This clause provides for the amendment of the First Schedule on projects that
require environmental and social impact assessment.
Clause 42

This clause repeals the current Second Schedule and substitute it with civil penalty
orders.
Clause 43

This clause repeals the Fourth Schedule.
Clause 44

This clause sets out additions in the Fifth Schedule of the list of invasive species.
(iii)
(iv)
Environmental Management Amendment
1
BILL
To provide for the amendment of the Environmental Management Act
[Chapter 20:27]; to provide for the incorporation of emerging
environmental principles; to provide for alignment with the Constitution
and give effect to environmental rights enshrined in the Constitution;
to further empower the Agency to effectively and efficiently carry out
its mandate; to provide for the further strengthening of the mandate to
protect and preserve the environment for present and future generations;
and to provide for matters connected with and incidental to the foregoing.

ENACTED by the Parliament and the President of Zimbabwe.
	 1
Short title

This Act may be cited as the Environmental Management (Amendment) Act, 2026.
	 2
Amendment of section 2 of Cap. 20:27

Section 2 (“Interpretation”) of the principal Act is amended—

(a)	 by the repeal of the definition of “environmental impact assessment”; and
the substitution of—

““environmental social management plan” means a comprehensive document
that outlines the strategies, mitigation measures, monitoring and
institutional arrangements required to manage environmental impacts
during project implementation;
1
Printed by the Government Printer, Harare
H.B. 5, 2026.]
5
10
15
20
Environmental Management Amendment
2

“environmental and social impact assessment” or “ESIA” means, in addition
to the environmental social management plan (which forms part of the
ESIA), a plan setting out the process by which (through consultations
with interested and affected stakeholders), the potential environmental
and social impacts of a proposed project may be predicted, assessed,
evaluated, mitigated, managed and monitored;

(b)	 in the definition of “environmental impact assessment report” by the
insertion after “environmental” of “and social”;

(c)	 in the definition of “waste” by the deletion of “radioactive form” and
anywhere else where there is a reference to “radiation” or “radioactive”
in the Act;

(d)	 by the deletion of the definition of “environmental audit” and the
substitution of—

“environmental audit” means a systematic, documented, periodic and
objective process in assessing compliance with relevant statutory and
internal requirements, thereby facilitating management control of
environmental practices;

(e)	 by the insertion of the following definitions—

“environmental service professionals” are persons or entities who have
knowledge, competencies and training necessary to give an expert
opinion or advice on the following fields—

(a)	 environmental planning and management;

(b)	 environmental economics;

(c)	 ecology and soil science;

(d)	 air, water and land pollution management and control;

(e)	 waste management;

(f)
hazardous substances;

(g)	 water and sanitation;

(h)	 land use planning;

(i)
environmental forensic auditing;

(j)
forestry management;

(k)	 bio-chemistry;

(l)
biodiversity and ecosystem management;

(m)	 geographical information systems;

(n)	 remote sensing and geo-informatics;

(o)	 climate change management;

(p)	 social ecology; or

(q)	 any other prescribed field of study or expertise associated with
relevant to environmental governance and compliance;

“priority waste” means specific waste streams which require specified
regulatory controls and duties, as they are prone to mismanagement
or are hazardous to human health or the environment;

“sustainable development” means development that meets the needs of the
present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet
their own needs;
2
5
10
15
20
25
30
35
40
45
Environmental Management Amendment
3

“small-scale projects” means a project with minimal or no mechanisation
and an anticipated low cost of setting up.”.
	 3
Amendment of section 4 of Cap. 20:27

Section 4 (“Environmental rights and principles of environmental management”) of
the principal Act is amended in subsection (2) by the insertion of the following paragraph
after paragraph (j)—

“(k)
any producer or distributor of priority waste must be responsible for
the waste management of his or her product throughout the product’s
life cycle.”.
	 4
Insertion of new sections of Cap. 20:27

The principal Act is amended by the insertion after section 4 of the following
sections—

“4A	Principles of environmental law enforcement


(1) The enforcement of this Act is based on the following
principles—

(a)	 the licensing by the Agency of social and economic activities
of natural and legal persons that potentially have the most
detrimental impact on the environment, with the view to
minimising or eliminating those effects;

(b)	 that natural and legal persons engaged in socially and
economically useful activities (whether licensed or not) that
have a detrimental environmental impact must in general,
engage in progressive rehabilitation to mitigate or eliminate
such environmental impact, the obligations of which will
(in the case of persons who engage in such activities as
an undertaking) be embodied in the environmental and
social impact assessment undertaken by those persons in
cooperation with the Agency;

(c)	 that natural and legal persons engaged in socially and
economically useful ongoing activities (whether licensed
or not) that have a detrimental environmental impact will,
upon a finding by the Agency, be subjected to civil penalty
orders to eliminate or minimise the detrimental impact
immediately or in the near future;

(d)	 that natural or legal persons that, as a result of their activities
cause serious damage to the environment resulting in actual
or potential serious harm to the health or safety or wellbeing
of human beings or biodiversity (whether such activities are
on-going or not or are licensed or not) will make reparation
and meet the cost to eliminate or mitigate the damage done,
based upon a monetary assessment by the Agency that is
enforced as an order of the court after conviction for the
offence relating to the causing of the serious damage in
question or pursuant to a non-prosecution agreement (polluter
pays principle);

(e)	 that activities conducted by natural or legal persons, whether
socially or economically useful, that involve an unacceptable
level of harm to human beings or biodiversity will be ordered
3
5
10
15
20
25
30
35
40
45
Environmental Management Amendment
4
to cease operations by the Agency upon a proper and fair
assessment of the risk involved.


(2) The Agency shall endeavour to use a range of flexible approaches to
ensure compliance, such as voluntary compliance mechanisms, economic or market-
based incentives, liability and legal or regulatory approaches.

4B	 General duty of care towards environment, and strict liability
for certain offences and special jurisdiction of magistrates’
courts


(1) Every person engaged in any environmental, social or economic
activity involving a real risk of harm to—

(a)	 the health and safety of human beings;

(b)	 biodiversity on an extensive scale; and

(c)	 the environment generally;


has a duty to ensure that appropriate measures are taken to prevent or
minimise any foreseeable harm that may result from such an activity.


(2) If any activity referred to in subsection (1) results in—

(a)	 the death or serious injury to human beings; or

(b)	 extensive lethal harm to biodiversity; or

(c)	 serious harm to any vital public interests; or

(d)	 extensive or irreparable harm to the livelihood of any
significant group of persons;


it shall constitute an offence, and—

  (i)	 in the absence of intention on the part of the accused
person, proof of negligence shall suffice for conviction;

 (ii)	 if intention or negligence on the part of the accused
person is proved, such person or in case of a corporate
person every member of the governing body of such

vii

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Wetlands management is the manipulation of an ecosystem to ensure maintenance of all
functions and characteristics of the specific wetland type. The wetland management involves
activities to manage, protect, restore, manipulate and provide for the functions and values,
emphasizing both quality and acreage by advocating for sustainable usage of them. Wetland
protection goals involve buffering wetlands from any direct human pressures that could affect
wetlands’ normal functions and also maintaining important natural processes that operate on them
that may be altered by human activities.

The importance of wetlands is, water storage, acting as natural earth sponges and are sources
of water for all rivers and streams. The importance also includes soaking up rain slowly and
recharging ground water, rivers and streams and water quality regulation through natural filtration.
They also provide habitat for plants and animals that live in semi aquatic conditions.

My audit was on protection of wetlands by the Environmental Management Agency (EMA). The
audit covered government designated wetlands and those under the Ramsar Convention. Ramsar
Convention on Wetlands is an international treaty for the conservation and sustainable use of
wetlands. The Agency is responsible for ensuring the sustainable management of natural
resources and the protection of the environment. EMA is a statutory body established under the
Environmental Management Act 13 of 2002 [Chapter 20:27]. The audit covered the period
January 01, 2014 to July 31, 2019. The audit was carried out in five provinces out of the ten.
The purpose of carrying out the audit was to assess whether the protection of the wetlands by
EMA was being done, efficiently and effectively.

My audit was motivated by requirements of the Constitution of Zimbabwe, Sustainable
Development Goals (SDGs), and local media reports on the degradation of wetlands.
According to Section 73 of the Constitution of Zimbabwe, every person has the right to an
environment that is not harmful to health and wellbeing. It also provides for the protection of
the environment for the benefit of present and future generations.

Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets 6.6 and 15.1 provide that by 2020,
governments should ensure the protection, conservation, restoration and sustainable use of
terrestrial and inland freshwater ecosystems and their services, in particular, wetlands, in
line with obligations under international agreements. Also SDG target 3.9 states that by 2030,
governments should have substantially reduced the number of deaths and illnesses caused
by water pollution.

I conducted the audit in accordance with International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions
(ISSAIs). I used documentary review, inspections and interviews to collect data in order to gain
an understanding of EMA processes on management and protection of wetlands.

Summary of Findings
There are many factors which determine the utilization of wetlands resulting in their possible
degradation. The main drivers of wetland degradation were governance issues, pollution by
untreated effluent, wetland cultivation and prescribed projects (construction and mining). The
causes of continued degradation of wetlands were inadequate enforcement of orders, inequitable
distribution of motor vehicles. The effects of wetland degradation were flash flooding, destruction
of flora and fauna, siltation and low levels of water table causing shortages of water.





viii

1. Governance issues
The National Environmental Council (NEC) was set up with the overall purpose of providing
advice on national goals and objectives and determining policies and priorities for the protection
of the environment. The Council is also tasked to produce the State of the Environment Report
(SOER) that is meant to help in determining the extent of the destruction of the environment over
a period of time. My audit revealed that the NEC last met in 2013. I also noted that the State of
the Environment Reports were produced in 1992, 1998, 2010 and 2017. However, the Agency
did not provide evidence that the 2010 and 2017 reports were tabled in Parliament. The fifth
edition was due in 2020. Furthermore, the State of the Environment Reports were not being
produced after every 5 years as required by Section 10 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27]. This
affected the effective management of wetlands.

Non- enforcement of the production and implementation of Local Environmental Action
Plans (LEAPs) by EMA
Every Local Authority should prepare a Local Environmental Action Plan (LEAP) for the area
under its jurisdiction in accordance with such directions as the Minister may give. The plans which
are supposed to be reviewed, evaluated and approved by EMA should include how the Local
Authority would manage and protect the environment including the wetlands. From the 74 local
authorities assessed by EMA in 2018, 36 had LEAP documents. However, out of the 36 local
authorities that developed the plans, only 11 were implementing them while the remaining 25 did
not implement or adhere to the plans.

Furthermore, my review of LEAP documents in the 5 visited provinces revealed that 28 Local
Authorities had LEAP documents and 21 had no such documents. In addition, out of the 28 with

ix

2. Pollution from discharge of untreated effluent
My audit noted that wetlands were being polluted by untreated effluent from local authorities,
individuals, mining operations and institutions in the 5 provinces I sampled. Out of 29 sewer
systems I inspected, 23 were not functioning as intended. I also noted that 6 individuals, 13 mining
companies and 24 institutions were discharging untreated effluent into wetlands. Untreated
effluent discharge by local authorities and companies into open areas was attributed to non-
functioning of effluent treatment systems while pollution by individuals was attributed to illegal
activities.

In addition, degradation of wetlands through pollution was also caused by:


Non-enforcement of submission of quarterly monitoring reports,

Ineffective inspections,

Delays to deliver samples to the EMAL,

Delays in analysing samples, and

Delays to provide feedback on tested samples to provinces by EMAL.

Non-enforcement of submission of quarterly monitoring reports
Developers were not submitting quarterly monitoring reports indicating the level and class of the
effluent they were discharging into wetlands. I sampled 43 developers and noted that only 10
were complying, 6 were partially complying and 27 were not complying. The non-submission of
quarterly monitoring reports by developers was due to inadequate enforcement by EMA.  The
effects of non-submission of quarterly monitoring reports were that the agency would not be able
to determine the extent of pollution of wetlands by developers. Audit however noted that the
system of waiting for reports from developers is not effective, rather EMA should be in the forefront
to monitor the activities.

Ineffective inspections
The agency was carrying out inspections of water and effluent discharge points and had been
surpassing inspection targets during the period under review. The inspections were done to
monitor pollution of wetlands. However, Midlands Province did not meet 2018 targets and
Mashonaland West Province did not meet 2016 and 2017 targets. Despite the Agency surpassing
inspection targets there was continued discharge of untreated effluent into wetlands due to
malfunctioning of treatment plants.

Delays to deliver samples to the Environmental Management Agency Laboratory (EMAL)
There were delays to deliver water samples to the laboratory for analysis by Masvingo,
Mashonaland West and Midlands Provinces. It was taking EMA Masvingo, Mashonaland West
and Midlands Provinces between 1 to 31 days to deliver samples to the laboratory against a
standard of a day. The delays to deliver samples to the EMAL may result in some samples being
exposed to contaminants which may distort the results.

Delays in analysing samples
The laboratory was experiencing delays in analysing water samples brought in to ascertain the
level of pollution. The time taken to analyse samples in the laboratory ranged between 9 to 70
days against a standard of 7 working days.








x

Delays to provide feedback on tested samples to provinces by EMAL
Documentary review of provincial sample records from 2014 to June 2019 revealed that the
laboratory was delaying to provide Masvingo, Mashonaland West, Matabeleland North and
Midlands provinces with feedback on samples analysed. The delays to provide feedback to the
four provinces ranged between 3 to 111 days. The most affected province was Midlands. There
were no delays to provide feedback to Harare Province since the EMAL and Harare provincial
offices were at the same complex.

The continued pollution has a negative impact on the wetlands as they would affect water quality
and destroy flora and fauna.

3. Wetland cultivation
I noted that there was cultivation of crops in wetlands and within 30 metres from the centre of the
rivers. This was more pronounced and uncontrolled in urban areas. Driefontein, Cleveland and
Monavale wetlands which are Ramsar designated sites were at threat from cultivation activities.
The Agency was not tracking the hectares affected by cultivation especially in the Ramsar
designated wetlands. Continued degradation of wetlands from cultivation activities was attributed
to non-issuance and non-enforcement of orders by EMA in the provinces that I visited. Cultivation
in wetlands may result in siltation and drying up of wetlands.

4. Prescribed projects (Construction and Mining)
Wetlands were also being destroyed by construction and mining activities. From the five provinces
I visited, construction of houses in wetlands occurred in Harare and Midlands provinces. The most
affected wetlands were Monavale a Ramsar designated wetland, Duri river in Chitungwiza,
Budiriro, Belvedere wetlands and Ascot wetland in Gweru.

Out of the five provinces visited, mining activities were more pronounced in Midlands,
Mashonaland West and Matabeleland North Provinces. I noted that some mining projects were
breaching the conditions of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) certificates. The mines were
encroaching into wetlands. The effects of mineral extraction on wetlands were drainage of wetland
areas, filling of wetlands with spoil, widening of stream beds, alteration of stream courses through
diversion and impoundment, increased silt load and turbidity, as well as decrease in both light
penetration and wetland habitat diversity.

The general causes of continued degradation of wetlands were:

Inadequate enforcement of orders,

Inequitable distribution of motor vehicles,

Non-alignment of Laws and Collaboration with other State Agencies

Inadequate enforcement of orders
EMA was not enforcing the orders issued to developers who were polluting wetlands by making
follows ups to ensure that corrective action had been taken. For the period under review 109
orders were issued but were not enforced.

Inequitable distribution of motor vehicles
I noted that the agency had 135 motor vehicles which were not equitably distributed among the
EMA provinces and districts. Head Office had 33% of the vehicles and 67% were shared among
8 provinces which translated into 7% per province. However, according to the distribution list





xi

Harare and Bulawayo provinces were not allocated vehicles. Harare Province was using vehicles
from Head Office whilst Bulawayo Province was sharing with Matabeleland North Province. The
vehicles were supposed to be used for environmental inspections awareness. This resulted in
District Environmental Officers (DEOs) operating without substantive vehicles as a result their
presence in communities was compromised.

Non-alignment of Laws and Collaboration with other State Agencies
I noted that there was limited support and participation from other law enforcing agents in terms
of protecting wetlands. It was also revealed that the EMA Act does not allow the Agency to
demolish structures illegally built on wetlands.

Recommendations
For EMA to sustainably protect the wetlands it should consider the following recommendations:

1. Enhance the governance issues by making sure that the National Environmental Council
becomes operational and the State of the Environment Report is produced and tabled in
parliament to provide information on the state of affairs. This will enable stakeholders to
monitor and come up with decisive actions to combat the destruction of the environment.
The National Environmental Council will enhance the coordination of environmental issues
so that strategic decisions are taken at national level.

2. Follow up with local authorities to ensure that Local Environment Action Plans (LEAPs)
are produced and implemented. Mechanisms need to be put in place through the parent
Ministries to ensure effective coordination. In addition, EMA through the Ministry of
Environment, Tourism and Hospitality Industry should lobby the Ministry of Local
Government and Public Works for funding of Local Authorities so that environmental
expertise is retained in Local Authorities. The production of LEAPs and their
implementation will go a long way in protecting the environment particularly stopping
degradation of wetlands from agricultural activities and pollution of wetlands in local
authorities.

3. Spearhead and coordinate through the parent Ministry engagements on wetlands
protection with key stakeholders particularly Ministry of Mines and Mining Development,
Ministry of Lands, Agriculture and Climate Change, Water and Rural Resettlement,
Ministry of Home Affairs and Cultural Heritage, Ministry of Justice, Legal and
Parliamentary Affairs and Ministry of Local Government and Public Works (Local
Authorities and Community Leadership). The coordination will enhance concerted efforts
to protect wetlands from continued pollution through construction, agricultural and mining
activities.

Furthermore, EMA should engage the parent Ministry to liaise with the Ministry of Justice,
Legal and Parliamentary Affairs for the swift redress of the law so that EMA is given the
power to enforce orders.

4. Enhance environmental inspections, enforcement of orders (with binding force of law
which allow penalties to be meted out) issued as well as conducting of regular
environmental audits for projects with EIA. The audits will enable EMA to check on
compliance with guidelines by stakeholders and taking of remedial action timeously. EMA
should also re-visit its vehicle distribution policy to capacitate the districts so that their





xii

presence in communities will be effective. This will go a long way in protecting the wetlands
in a sustainable manner.

5. Enforce the submission of quarterly monitoring reports by developers. This will help EMA
to monitor the quality and quantity of effluent discharged by developers. Plan for physical
inspections should be in place and adhered to at all times.

6. Expedite the delivery and analysis of water samples and provide feedback to provinces
on analysed water samples. Timely delivery and analysis of water samples and giving
feedback to provinces will improve the sustainable protection of wetlands when decisions
are made in time. Considerations should also be made to decentralize some of the
operations to facilitate efficiencies and effectiveness.

7. Revisit laws and regulations with the aim of coming up with a clear position on overall
responsibility and eliminate overlaps. Stringent deterrent measures to would be offenders
should also be put in place to reduce cases of repeat offenders. The environment needs
to be preserved for the current and future generations.

1 Introduction

1.1 Background
My audit was on protection of wetlands by the Environmental Management Agency (EMA). The
Agency is responsible for ensuring the sustainable management of natural resources and the
protection of the environment. EMA is a statutory body established under the Environmental
Management Act 13 of 2002 [Chapter 20:27].

A wetland is any area of marsh1, fen2, peatland3 or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent
or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, and includes riparian4 land
adjacent to the wetland. The wetland management involves activities to manage, protect, restore,
manipulate and provide for the functions and values, emphasizing both quality and acreage by
advocating for sustainable usage of them. Management goals involve buffering wetlands from
any direct human pressures that could affect wetlands’ normal functions and also maintaining
important natural processes that operate on them that may be altered by human activities.

According to EMA, the following are the importance of wetlands;
i.
Water storage.
ii.
Act as natural earth sponges and are sources of water for all rivers and streams.
iii.
Soak up rain slowly and recharge ground water, rivers and streams.
iv.
Help in flood protection by absorbing excess water.
v.
Water quality regulation through natural filtration.
vi.
Provide habitat for plants and animals that live in semi aquatic conditions.
vii.
Economic recreational and cultural functions (including hiking, fishing, bird watching,
photography and hunting).

Zimbabwe is a signatory to The Ramsar Convention (United Nations Treaty number 145830)
which is an inter-governmental treaty to promote national action and international co-
operation for the conservation and wise use of wetlands and their resources. Zimbabwe
entered into the convention on May 3, 2013. A total of 7 sites in Zimbabwe have been
designated as ‘Ramsar protected wetlands’ covering 28 582.40 hectares. EMA is mandated to
protect and monitor all the wetlands. The 7 sites are Victoria Falls, Cleveland Dam, Lake Chivero,
Middle Zambezi/Mana Pools, Chinhoyi caves, Monavale Vlei and Driefontein Grasslands.
However, according to an EMA Wetlands Status Report (2019), there are 1136 government
designated wetlands within the country’s borders which cover about 3% of the total surface area.

environment for the benefit of present and future generations.

Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets 6.6 and 15.1 provide that by 2020,
governments should ensure the protection, conservation, restoration and sustainable use of

1.5 Organisational structure
Environment Management Agency is run by the Environmental Management Board which

ecology, pollution, waste management, soil science, hazardous substances, water, sanitation,
and a registered legal practitioner.

The EMA Laboratory supports and advises on all aspects of environmental quality such as

1.8 Audit questions and assessment criteria

AQ.1 To what extent is EMA monitoring wetlands pollution from effluent discharge?

AC.1 According to Section 36 (c) of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], the Director-General, inspectors
and other officers should ensure, that pollution and degradation of land and water is avoided,
minimized, managed or regulated, so far as is practicable and permissible to do so under any law.

AQ.1.1 Is EMA enforcing submission of quarterly environmental monitoring reports by
developers?

AC.1.1 According to Section 13 (2) of Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007, EMA should ensure that
developers submit quarterly environmental monitoring reports on any issues raised in the
environmental impact assessment report or any other issues that arise as a result of the
implementation of the project. Failure to submit quarterly reports will make the developer liable to
a fine not exceeding level 14 or imprisonment for 12 months or both fine and imprisonment.

AQ.1.2. To what extent is transportation and delivery of water samples impacting on
timeous analysis of samples?

AC.1.2 According to the EMAL SOP number 14, samples should be taken by district officers to
the EMAL within 24 hours of collection.

AQ.1.3 To what extent is analysis and reporting results of water samples affecting
monitoring of wetlands by EMA?

AC.1.3 According to the EMAL SOP revision number 14, the turnaround time from the day a
sample is received until the results are communicated to respective provinces should be 7 working
days.

AQ.1.4 To what extent is stock management of reagents impacting on testing of samples?

AC.1.4 According to EMAL SOP revision number 14 item number 5.2.4, before a test is
conducted, the Quality Steering Committee should ensure that there are adequate reagents and
consumables. Furthermore, good stock management requires that buffer stocks should always
be available to ensure continuity of operations.

AQ.1.5 Does the EMAL repair equipment on time for testing samples?

AC.1.5 According to EMAL SOP revision number 14 item 5.5.8, malfunctioning equipment should
be repaired on time.

AQ.2 To what extent is EMA monitoring wetlands degradation from cultivation activities?

AC.2 According to Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007, Section 20 (1), through monitoring, EMA should
ensure that no person, without a license issued by the Agency cultivate or license the cultivation
of wetlands.

before commencement in wetlands?

AC.3 According to Section 97 (1) (a) as red with the first schedule of the EMA Act

AQ.3.1 To what extent is EMA carrying out bi-annual environmental audits to monitor
pollution of wetlands?

AC.3.1 According to Section 13 (1) of Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007, the Agency should carry
out bi-annual environmental audits of prescribed projects to ensure that all projects being
implemented are in compliance with the regulations.

AQ.4 Are orders issued by EMA being enforced?

AC.4.1 According to Section 114(10) of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], any person who refuses or

AC.4.1 According to EMA management, vehicles are required to ensure mobility of inspectors

AC.5 According to Section 7 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], there should be a National

AQ.6 Is EMA facilitating the compilation and production of the State of the Environment

AC.6 According to Section 10 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], EMA should co-ordinate the

AQ.7 Is EMA facilitating production and implementation of LEAPs by local authorities?

AC.7 According to Section 10(1) of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], EMA should develop guidelines

2.6 Enforcement for protection of wetlands
Section 113 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27] states that the Minister may declare any wetland to
be an ecologically sensitive area and may impose limitations on development in or around such
area. No person should except in accordance with the express written authorization of the Agency
given in consultation with the Board and the Minister responsible for water resources;

reclaim or drain any wetland,

disturb any wetland by drilling or tunneling in a manner that has or is likely to have an
adverse impact on any wetland or adversely affect any animal or plant life therein, and

introduce any exotic animal or plant species into the wetland.
Furthermore, Section 114 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27] states that an order may be issued to
those who contravene the requirements of Section 113 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27]. According
to Section 115 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], an Inspector may make an order for protection of
the environment if s/he considers that it is necessary to act immediately.

2.8 Ecological Assessment
Samples are collected every month at source by the Provincial Environmental Officer (PEO) using
the correct sampling technique.  The Sampler arranges for transport before sampling to ensure
delivery of the samples to the Environmental Management Agency Laboratory (EMAL) within 24
hours. An analyst comes up with the test method, tests the sample and records the results. The
results are then dispatched to the district in the form of hard copy or by electronic mode. The
turnaround time for testing the samples is 7 working days and is counted from the day the sample
is received until the report is ready for collection or e-mailing. The counting excludes weekends.

2.8.1 Planned maintenance and service of EMAL Equipment
According to EMAL Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) number 14 of 2017, EMAL procures
modern and up to date instruments and quality products all the time. The maintenance of
equipment follows the relevant equipment maintenance procedures for that piece of equipment.
EMAL designs a service schedule for equipment in the laboratory in the first quarter of the year.
If equipment is not performing according to standard, it is reported to the Area Supervisor. If the
calibration of the equipment is valid, the equipment is recommended for servicing. It is recorded
on the fault form FM30/QA.






15

On completion of servicing or repair of equipment, it should be calibrated. All equipment to be
calibrated should be recorded in the calibration form and a calibration schedule is prepared.
Quotations must be sought from competent calibration laboratories and a supplier is chosen from
the quotations. A calibration certificate bearing traceability should be issued after every
calibration. Certificates of calibration should be filed in the calibrations file. A sticker should be
attached to the equipment calibrated stating the date of calibration and the next calibration date.

CHAPTER 3


3 Findings
This chapter details my findings on protection of wetlands by EMA. There are many factors which
determine the utilization of wetlands resulting in their possible degradation. The main drivers of
wetland degradation were governance issues, pollution by untreated effluent, wetland cultivation
and prescribed projects (construction and mining). The causes of continued degradation of
wetlands were inadequate enforcement of orders, inequitable distribution of motor vehicles. The
effects of wetland degradation were flash flooding, destruction of flora and fauna, siltation and low
levels of water table causing shortages of water.

3.1 Governance issues
My audit revealed that there was weak governance in the protection of the environment
(wetlands). This was evidenced by non-conducting of business by the National Environmental
Council as expected and State of the Environment Reports were not being produced after every
5 years as required by Section 10 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27].

3.1.1 Non-conducting of business by the National Environmental Council
According to Section 7 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], there should be established a council to
be known as the National Environmental Council. The Council should meet at least 4 times in
every financial year, at such place as it may deem appropriate for the transaction of its business.
The following are the functions of the Council;
i.
to advise on national goals and objectives and determine policies and priorities for the
protection of the environment,
ii.
to promote co-operation among public departments, local authorities, private sector, non-
governmental organizations and such other organizations engaged in environmental
protection programs,
iii.
to make recommendations to all appropriate persons and authorities regarding the
harmonization of functions related to the environment,
iv.
to review and recommend to the Minister guidelines for environmental management plans
and environmental action plans,
v.
to review and recommend incentives for the protection of the environment, and
vi.
to review the national environmental plan.

According to interviews with EMA management, it was revealed that the council was established
and last met on July 22, 2013. Since then the council had not been active. All the functions and
goals of the council were not met because it was not effective, hence issues to do with wetland
protection were not being addressed.

Management response
The National Environmental Council (NEC) held its first meeting on July 2013 and another
one in 2018. However, turn out at Secretary level was low at both meetings.
With the involvement of the Office of the President and Cabinet, alternate, but senior
nominations were sought and finalized in 2019. Names of the Members were to be gazetted
and were submitted to the Attorney General’s Office. However, the COVID-19 pandemic hit
the country before the NEC could meet in 2020 to date.

Meetings will definitely resume once COVID-19 protocols are removed.

 3.1.2 State of the Environment report
According to Section 10 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27], EMA should co-ordinate the production
of a report on the state of the environment every five years. The report should be tabled in
parliament.

According to documentary review of the last published State of the Environment Reports and
interviews with key personnel at EMA, I noted that the State of the Environment Reports were
produced in 1992, 1998, 2010 and 2017. However, the Agency did not provide evidence that the
2010 and 2017 reports were tabled in Parliament. The fifth edition was due in 2020. Furthermore,
the State of the Environment Reports were not being produced after every 5 years as required by
Section 10 of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27].



The effect of not tabling the State of the Environment Reports is that the nation and key
stakeholders would not be able to track the extent of the destruction of the environment over a
period of time.

Management response
The 2017 State of the Environmental report was submitted to Parliament on July 15, 2019.

The Harare Provincial Manager indicated that the Local Authorities were simply not complying in
producing LEAP documents despite that workshops and trainings were carried out yearly by EMA.
From my review of the National Evaluation Report (2018), I noted that non-production of LEAPs
was attributed to the fact that local authorities did not have correctly constituted environmental
committees. According to EMA guidelines, the environmental committee for local authorities were
supposed to have at least one committee member with an environmental qualification or relevant
experience. The committee members with environmental qualifications would provide technical
expertise on how environmental issues should be managed in local authorities. Out of the 74 local
authorities evaluated, only 12 had correctly constituted environmental committees to spearhead
LEAPs production. This was partially due to lack of funding. This is the reason why some local
authorities were not producing LEAPs. In the case of Victoria Falls Municipality, management
revealed that non-production of the LEAP document was as a result of high staff turnover.

On non-implementation by Local Authorities which had produced the plans, I noted from the
Evaluation Report that trivialisation of environmental issues and lack of funding were the main
causes. This was evidenced by lack of correctly constituted environmental committees for local
authorities and lack of participation by traditional leaders.  Lack of participation by traditional
leaders was highlighted in the LEAP Evaluation Report which indicated that less than 30% of
traditional leaders were active in environmental management activities.

Non-production and non-implementation of these plans by local authorities may result in
continued degradation of the environment including wetlands.

Management response
The Agency has engaged Ministry of Local Government to resource the component of the
LEAP through budgets to enable its implementation.

3.2.4.1 Non-enforcement of submission of quarterly monitoring reports
According to Section 13 (2) of Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007, EMA should ensure that developers
submit quarterly environmental monitoring reports on any issues raised in the environmental
impact assessment report or any other issues that arise as a result of the implementation of the
project. Failure to submit quarterly reports will make the developer liable to a fine not exceeding
level 14 or imprisonment for 12 months or both fine and imprisonment.

My review of water and effluent licence registers from the five provinces I visited during the period
under review revealed that only 10 out of 43 developers were consistently submitting quarterly
monitoring reports, 27 did not submit and 6 were inconsistently submitting. Refer to Annexure I
for details.

Management response
The Agency acknowledges the observation of non-submission of quarterly reports
in terms of Section 13(2) of Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007. The Annexure I referred
comprise mainly of sewer treatment facilities, pump stations and projects that
existed before the enactment of the EMA Act [Chapter 20:27]. However, Section
13(2) applies to submission of quarterly reports for projects issued with EIA
certificates in terms of Section 100.  Out of that list, only thirteen (13) projects are
subject to quarterly reports in terms of Section 13(2) of Statutory Instrument 7 of
2007.  These are Glow Petroleum, Lafarge Cement, Peakwood Investments, Danbro
Holdings, Zimplats SMC, Zimplats Ngezi, Hwange Colliery, Makomo Resources,
ZPC Hwange, Zambezi Crocs, Makomo Resources, Emthunzini Housing Development and
Delta Fairbridge.

The remaining projects listed on Annexure I are subject to Section 9(6) of Statutory
Instrument 6 of 2007 which require submission of quarterly reports for monitoring
purposes and use during quarterly billing. Failure to submit the report results in
classification in a default yellow class.

For projects that are subjected to Section 13(2) on quarterly reports, penalties for non-
submission of quarterly reports are issued during audits as well as at EIA renewal stages
as it is a precondition for EIA renewal.

3.2.4.3 Delays to deliver samples to the Environmental Management Agency Laboratory
(EMAL)
According to the EMAL Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) number 14, samples extracted for
pollution testing should be taken to the EMAL within 24 hours of collection to avoid contamination
before testing.
I noted that there were delays to deliver water samples to the laboratory for analysis by Masvingo,
Mashonaland West and Midlands provinces. It was taking these provinces between 1 to 31 days
to deliver samples to the laboratory. Refer to Annexure J.  The delays were attributed to shortage
of vehicles in the provinces. These delays to deliver samples to the EMAL may have resulted in
some of the samples being exposed to contaminants thereby distorting the results.

Documentary review of sample registers for the period from 2014 to June 2019 in Matabeleland
North Province revealed that there were no delays to deliver water samples to the EMAL. The
province was managing to deliver water samples to the EMAL within 24 hours of collection from
the sampling points.

Management Response
The Agency acknowledges the observation. The contributing factor is shortage of
vehicles. Vehicle distribution does not apply to samples only but the whole organization
and its operations in its entirety. The Agency is in the process of recapitalization in terms
of vehicles. In 2019 and 2020, the mentioned provinces have been beefed up with one land
cruiser, one Land Rover Defender and one NP200 Nissan each. In addition to alternatives
in trying to ensure samples are delivered on time, Masvingo Province has initiated the use
of Swift Courier for overnight delivery. The approach will be rolled out to all provinces
which are a distant from the Laboratory. Currently the Agency is considering
decentralizing the laboratory services by establishing satellite laboratories in Bulawayo





30

and Mutare. The Bulawayo laboratory is already at an advanced stage. In addition, the
property had been acquired and architectural designs are already in place.

3.2.4.4 Delays in analyzing samples
According to the EMAL SOP revision number 14, the turnaround time from the day a sample is
received until the results are communicated to the respective provinces should be 7 working days.

I observed that the laboratory was experiencing delays to analyse water samples brought in to
ascertain the level of pollution. The time taken to analyse samples in the laboratory ranged
between 9 to 70 days. Refer to Annexure K for more details. Delays in analysing samples was
due to:

Stock outs of reagents and

Obsolescence of laboratory equipment.

Management Response
According to laboratory records, samples received in December 2018 were affected by
metal analysis which could not be done because of shortage of acetylene gas for Atomic
absorption spectrometer. Metal analysis stopped on December 13, 2018 and was only
resumed on February 5, 2019. The gas was not available at BOC gases.

The turnaround time for most internal samples was also affected by the increase in
workload during the period 1st to the 7th ambient period of the month where over 200
samples were received and required analysis at the same time. The turnaround time for
the internal samples was then increased to 10 working days but remained a challenge.

Management had already put in place five reserved Acetylene tanks; however,
management have no mechanism to control foreign payments in times of national crisis.
Management has put on the Public Sector Investment Programmes (PSIP), a budget of
USD450 000 for purchasing an Inductively Coupled Plasma-MS-TOF that processes all
metals from Hydrogen to Uranium (All elements of the periodic table) in 10-30 seconds as
compared to the current Atomic Absorption Spectrometer which takes longer to analyse
samples.

3.2.4.5 Stock outs of laboratory reagents
According to EMAL SOP revision number 14 item number 5.2.4, the Quality Steering Committee
should ensure that there are adequate reagents and consumables all the time. Furthermore, good
stock management requires that buffer stocks should always be available to ensure continuity of
operations.
I observed that the laboratory was experiencing stock outs of reagents used to test samples of
water during the period from January 2014 to June 2019.  The stock outs period ranged between
20 to 901 days. Refer to Annexure L for details. The stock outs of laboratory reagents resulted in
delays in analysing samples.  The delays could have had an effect on the final results due to
changes in the state of the sample.

Management response
The greater chunk of the chemicals and reagents mentioned in Annex 1 are slow-moving.
and they take a maximum of about 3 years to expire. A good example is the mercury
standard which according to laboratory records was in stock on 01/09/15 when the annual
stock take was done. This standard was taken out to the laboratory for use on 02/02/16,





31

meaning the balance recorded in the stores department was zero. This standard was not
replaced immediately because it is used over a long period of time.

According to laboratory records there were test reports that could not be produced due to
stocked out chemicals and reagents during the time frame mentioned. Management will
strive to improve the system by strengthening re-order levels especially for analytical
standards and slow-moving reagents.

3.2.4.6 Obsolete laboratory equipment
Documentary review and an interview held with the EMAL Manager, revealed that the laboratory
had obsolete equipment during the period from January 2014 to June 2019 when I visited the
laboratory.  As a result, the processing speed of the machines was slow.  Annexure M has details
of obsolete equipment. The equipment needed to be replaced with more modern equipment which
has readily available spares and speed in processing samples.

The equipment listed in Annexure M was inherited from the ZINWA laboratory Water Pollution
Unit. The unit was transferred to EMA in 2003 resulting in the formation of the EMAL. The agency
seems not to have been including in its budgets the issue of the procurement of new equipment.
The use of obsolete equipment might result in delays to analyse samples, delays to provide
feedback to provinces, and some analysis not being done.

Management response
Most of the equipment were inherited from ZINWA already not working. EMA has since
replaced all the equipment in Annexure M except for the Oxygen gauge E12/2440 and
Oxygen 200 bar surface gauge 999 respectively that still belong to ZINWA. Therefore, 91%
of all malfunctioning equipment that were inherited from ZINWA by Environmental
Management Agency Laboratory were replaced.

The processing speed of the existing equipment that is working in the laboratory is in line
with the design or make up of the equipment which cannot be changed. However, with
increasing environmental samples, faster sample processing equipment is desired
especially for the bigger machines that processes many parameters per time. In addition,
management is working towards the disposal of all non-working equipment and
purchasing new equipment.

Management is working towards a central email in provincial registry for receiving and

Inadequate environmental audits
