According to Section 13 (1) of the Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007, the Agency should carry out bi-
annual environmental audits of prescribed projects19 to ensure that all projects being implemented
are in compliance with the regulations.

According to inspection report at Harare Province I noted that 16 projects were granted
permission to utilize wetlands (W1-Wet for relatively short and infrequent periods). Thirteen of
them had started construction activities. EMA was supposed to carry out bi-annual environmental
audits on these projects. However, there was no evidence that EMA carried out these audits for
the period 2014 to May 2019. Details of the projects are in Annexure P.

In Midlands Province African Chrome Fields (ACF) Mine was granted EIA to utilize W1 wetland
in 2016. EMA was supposed to carry out bi-annual audits for the mining company from 2016.
However, the agency only carried out environmental audits once a year instead of twice a year.
The major environmental issues in the reports were that ACF was polluting both surface and
underground water through its operations.

The effects of not carrying out bi-annual environmental audits were that it was not possible to
ascertain whether or not the approved conditions of project were implemented. Furthermore,
without carrying out the bi-annual environmental audits, these pollution cases can go unidentified
and may not be addressed on time to save the environment. Also it would be difficult to test the
accuracy of the impact prediction and effectiveness of mitigation measures to protect wetlands.

Management response
The 16 projects in Harare Province were granted with EIA certificates since the projects
were prescribed within the First Schedule of the Act.

Auditor’s evaluation
Even though the projects were granted with EIA, the environmental audits were not done in terms
of section 13 (1) of Statutory Instrument 7 of 2007 which requires that the Agency should carry
out bi-annual environmental audits of prescribed projects to ensure that all projects being
implemented are in compliance with the regulations.

3.5.3 Non-alignment of Laws and Collaboration with other State Agencies
Through review of the EMA Strategic Plan for 2013 to 2018 it was noted that there was limited
support and participation from other law enforcing agents in terms of protecting wetlands. From
interviews with the EMA Harare Provincial Manager it was revealed that the EMA Act does not
allow the Agency to demolish structures illegally built on wetlands. The Town Planning Act
[Chapter 29:12] administered by the local authorities Section 35 gives authority to demolish to
local authorities and not EMA. This therefore posed challenges when coordinating with Local
Authorities as they will be reluctant to do so for unspecified reasons to demolish structures on
wetlands.

Management response
The re-alignment of the legislation is the responsibility of the Ministry of Environment,
Climate, Tourism and Hospitality Industry and is currently being done through the Ministry.
However, we have since submitted our suggestions to be incorporated in the Principal Act
amendments in the year 2018.

The Agency is now member of the one-stop shop housed at Town Council for the
assessment and approval of development plans, change of land use approval and
subdivisions approval so as to improve wetlands management in a coordinated approach.

CHAPTER 4

4.0 Conclusions
Below are general and specific conclusions pertaining to my audit on management of Wetlands
by EMA.

4.1 General conclusion
EMA has challenges in efficiently and effectively protecting wetlands as evidenced by continued
degradation of wetlands through pollution, cultivation, construction and mining.

4.2 Specific conclusions
The following are specific conclusions:
4.2.1 There are weak governance issues in the protection of the environment (wetlands). This
is evidenced by non-conducting of business by the National Environmental Council and
inconsistent production of the State of the Environment Report.

4.2.2 EMA is not effectively controlling the pollution of wetlands by the various parties.
Wetlands are being polluted by untreated effluent discharge from local authorities, mining and
industrial companies and individual activities. Most rivers and streams in local authorities are
flowing with untreated effluent discharged from malfunctioning sewer systems perennially. The
government may fail to achieve SDG goal 6.3 of improving water quality by reducing pollution by
2030 if the issue of pollution of wetlands is not addressed. Also EMA was ineffective in carrying
out environmental inspection and testing water and soil samples for pollution.

4.2.3 EMA has not been able to stop wetland cultivation due to non-issuance and enforcement
of orders to stop streambank and wetlands cultivation. This is most pronounced in urban local
authorities especially in Harare. If the practice is not stopped immediately all wetlands will be
destroyed due to cultivation activities. This is resulting in siltation of rivers and drying up of
wetlands. The government may fail to achieve SDG Goal 6.6 which requires it to protect and
restore water-related ecosystems by 2020.

4.2.4 Wetlands are being destroyed by illegal housing and infrastructural development. This
challenge is more prevalent in Harare metropolitan province and its surroundings. Even the
Ramsar designated wetlands have not been spared. There is inadequate coordination between
EMA and local authorities when issuing land for housing developments and mining.  Local
Authorities are allocating land for development on wetlands without consulting the Agency. On
the other hand, EMA has not succeeded in stopping some developers from building and mining
on wetlands before they get EIA certificates that set out the operating guidelines. This has been
exacerbated by the fact that EMA does not have the powers to demolish illegal structures.









48

Chapter 5

5 RECOMMENDATIONS

For EMA to sustainably protect the wetlands it should consider the following recommendations:

1. Enhance the governance issues by making sure that the National Environmental Council
becomes operational and the State of the Environment Report is produced and tabled in
parliament to provide information on the state of affairs. This will enable stakeholders to
monitor and come up with decisive actions to combat the destruction of the environment.
The National Environmental Council will enhance the coordination of environmental issues
so that strategic decisions are taken at national level.

2. Follow up with local authorities to ensure that Local Environment Action Plans (LEAPs)
are produced and implemented. Mechanisms need to be put in place through the parent
Ministries to ensure effective coordination. In addition, EMA through the Ministry of
Environment, Tourism and Hospitality Industry should lobby the Ministry of Local
Government and Public Works for funding of Local Authorities so that environmental
expertise is retained in Local Authorities. The production of LEAPs and their
implementation will go a long way in protecting the environment particularly stopping
degradation of wetlands from agricultural activities and pollution of wetlands in local
authorities.

3. Spearhead and coordinate through the parent Ministry engagements on wetlands
protection with key stakeholders particularly Ministry of Mines and Mining Development,
Ministry of Lands, Agriculture and Climate Change, Water and Rural Resettlement,
Ministry of Home Affairs and Cultural Heritage, Ministry of Justice, Legal and
Parliamentary Affairs and Ministry of Local Government and Public Works (Local
Authorities and Community Leadership). The coordination will enhance concerted efforts
to protect wetlands from continued pollution through construction, agricultural and mining
activities.

Furthermore, EMA should engage the parent Ministry to liaise with the Ministry of Justice,
Legal and Parliamentary Affairs for the swift redress of the law so that EMA is given the
power to enforce orders.

4. Enhance environmental inspections, enforcement of orders (with binding force of law
which allow penalties to be meted out) issued as well as conducting of regular
environmental audits for projects with EIA. The audits will enable EMA to check on
compliance with guidelines by stakeholders and taking of remedial action timeously. EMA
should also re-visit its vehicle distribution policy to capacitate the districts so that their
presence in communities will be effective. This will go a long way in protecting the wetlands
in a sustainable manner.

5. Enforce the submission of quarterly monitoring reports by developers. This will help EMA
to monitor the quality and quantity of effluent discharged by developers. Plan for physical
inspections should be in place and adhered to at all times.






49

6. Expedite the delivery and analysis of water samples and provide feedback to provinces
on analysed water samples. Timely delivery and analysis of water samples and giving
feedback to provinces will improve the sustainable protection of wetlands when decisions
are made in time. Considerations should also be made to decentralize some of the
operations to facilitate efficiencies and effectiveness.

7. Revisit laws and regulations with the aim of coming up with a clear position on overall
responsibility and eliminate overlaps. Stringent deterrent measures to would be offenders
should also be put in place to reduce cases of repeat offenders. The environment needs
to be preserved for the current and future generations.
